newsitem.title: USA: Paula Jones, from Lonoke, Arkansas to Supreme Court.
newsitem.headline: Paula Jones, from Lonoke, Arkansas to Supreme Court.

text.p: Paula Corbin Jones, who sued U.S. President Bill Clinton for sexual harassment, grew up in a factory town outside Little Rock, Arkansas, one of three sisters raised in a strict Christian household.

From her early days in Lonoke, Arkansas, population about 4,000, Jones entered the national limelight in 1994, when she held a news conference in Washington telling of her accusations against Clinton.

At the February 11, 1994, conference, which was organised by the Conservative Political Action Conference, Jones said Clinton, then governor of Arkansas, had asked her for "a type of sex" when the two were alone in an Arkansas hotel room on May 8, 1991.

Newsweek magazine quoted her as telling one reporter on another occasion: "I will never forget the look on his face ... His face was just red, beet red." She said Clinton complimented her on her hair and "curves" and then drew her close to "nibble" her neck.
Jones said Clinton lowered his trousers and told her to "kiss it," the January, 1997 Newsweek article reported, adding she responded by jumping up and saying "Look, I'm not that kind of girl."
Clinton denied her allegations. The Supreme Court made no ruling on Tuesday on the merits of her case, but said the lawsuit should be allowed to proceed through the judicial system.
Jones, then a $12,000-a-year clerical worker for the Arkansas Industrial Development Commission, was at the hotel because she was asked to help at a conference.
In 1994, following the news conference and after months of negotiations with Clinton's attorney, Robert Bennett, Jones filed a lawsuit seeking $700,000 in damages.

She said then she wanted an apology from the president to clear her name. After the Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday that the case could proceed while Clinton was in the White House, Jones' lawyers said again she wanted her good name restored.

Jones contended she took the legal action to clear her name after American Spectator published an article claiming Arkansas state policemen set up sexual liaisons for Clinton. One of the women in the article was identified by the name "Paula." Jones alleged this tied her to the case.

A month after filing the lawsuit, Jones promoted "No Excuses" sportswear at a New York news conference. The clothing firm previously attracted attention with such models as Donna Rice, whose liaison with former Senator Gary Hart of Colorado contributed to his political troubles.

Later in 1994, Penthouse magazine published photographs of Jones wearing only a G-string that she said she allowed a boyfriend to take in 1987 on the understanding that they would be kept private. Jones tried and failed to stop distribution of the issue that contained the photographs.

Jones grew up in Lonoke. According to the Washington Post, the household was run along strict religious principles, with the daughters forbidden to wear jewelry, have stylish haircuts or watch television.
She graduated from nearby Carlisle High School. Her father worked at a nearby sewing factory while her mother did not work outside the home, the Post reported.
Now 30, Jones lives with her husband, Steve Jones, an airlines reservations clerk, and two sons in Long Beach, California.
